E1536.summary: One of the three principles (with Sulphur and Mercury); identified by Atwood with Will, Wisdom and the Root of Reason, and by quoted adepts as the most ancient principle of the Stone.
E1536.body:
Salt is one of the three principles with Sulphur and Mercury; Atwood lists it third in the series of [III.1 ¶53], in the same position as the body principle and the proceeding substance (how these relate is left open), and the Adept she cites says “yet without Salt no man can attain to this Sacred Science” [III.1 ¶61]. In Sendivogius's fable “Sal gave Sulfur a mortal wound” [III.1 ¶56].

**Atwood's identifications.** In the main text she speaks of the Saturnian Salt which, developed to intellect and made erect, subdues all nature, equating it with “the internal spiritual Sun which is the Perpetual Motion of the Wise, and that Saturnian Salt” [II.3 ¶52], and with “that Salt which the Savior orders that we should have it in ourselves” [II.3 ¶54]. She calls it “that saving Salt which philosophers were wont anciently to excavate and by so many circulating media to exalt”, identifying it with the Root of Reason and Wisdom: “this same Root of Reason is Wisdom, and that saving Salt” [IV.4 ¶20].

**Appendix (Table Talk, later layer).** Salt = Will: “There is no true body but Will; it is the principle of the body --- the Salt.” [APP ¶65]. “The Slat is the voluntary substance”, bound in the generative mineral life; drawn up into the medial life, “the Salt thus transplanted becomes Light and grows” [APP ¶77]. “The Salt, the will, opens it secondfold.” [APP ¶182] (the sense of ‘secondfold’ is unclear).

**Quoted voices.** The mysterious adeptest calls it “Salt, that most ancient principle of the Stone” and “The Salt of Saturn, the Universal son of Nature”, “always and everywhere universal through its own fusibility, self-existent in nature”; “not without weighty cause has Salt been dignified with the name of Wisdom”; its nucleus in the Decad is to be kept secret; with the Sun, it is that “than which, together with the Sun, nothing is found more useful” [III.3 ¶50]. The Adept speaks of an immortal Salt in the mind's machinery, “that marvelous Salt, which is that menstruum in the sphere of Saturn mentioned by Eirenaeus, which can calcine gold” [IV.2 ¶30]. Vaughan mentions “three Argent vives and as many Salts” without explanation [IV.2 ¶35].

E1537.summary: The most abstruse principle of the Stone: deprived of light, the central earth whose perpetual motion emanates the first material universe; identified with Demogorgon and the mineral soul.
E1537.body: In a passage whose voice is unclear, “The Salt of Saturn, that most abstruse principle of the Stone --- the most ancient Demogorgon” [II.3 ¶41] is said to be deprived of light, the one “whose perpetual motion emanates the first material universe, and is the mineral soul” [II.3 ¶41]. It is also the central earth whose Being is Tartarus: “This is the earth, distinguished by Anaxagoras, which abiding durably in the center” [II.3 ¶41]. Compare Salt, where a quoted adept calls the Salt of Saturn the “Universal son of Nature” [III.3 ¶50].

E1538.summary: In the Lucerna Solis verse, the Sages' name for the one universal thing containing all nature and Life, extracted from their earth, and not vulgar salt.
E1538.body: Quoted from the Lucerna Solis: the one universal thing, present everywhere, containing all nature and all Life and extracted from ‘their earth’, is known only to the Sages: “The band of Sages only have known it, And they call it their salt.” It is explicitly not common salt: “Nor the vulgar salt in any manner, But rather the salt of the world” [I.2 ¶10].

E1539.summary: The three principles of the Adepts: modes of being of one Matter, related as agent, patient and offspring; not the literal substances chemists misapplied.
E1539.body:
**Atwood.** Literal chemists failed to extract the Form of gold “by salt, sulfur and mercury, or the three combined with antimony” [I.1 ¶86]. Properly, “The three principles, the Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury, are merely different as modes of being of the same thing” [I.2 ¶39], exhibited by nature from the Matter's unity after the annihilate condition, as agent, patient and offspring. They are contained in the first matter of metals, a doctrine “of which so much has been spoken and ignorantly misapplied” [I.3 n22]; they are “the paternal, maternal, and proceeding ens of life. And there are the Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury of the Adepts” [I.3 n30]; “thou hast in these three principles, says Sendivogius, a body, a spirit, and an occult soul” [I.3 n30]. Per Vaughan they are hidden intrinsical natures, not literal ‘pot-principles’ [I.3 n30]. At [III.3 ¶77] she names them “the Sulphur and Mercury and Slat, the active and the passive, and the resulting experience of life”: “The first, I the regeneration, is the Word of God independent without all human will”; “the second is of the Humanity, i.e., of the selfhood, prepared and sanctified”; “the result of these two in unison is the Bodily Substance of things thenceforth created” — three powers in one seat. In the mind's machinery she lists “wheel within wheel revolving vitally, Mercury, Sulphur, and an immortal Salt” [IV.2 ¶30]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer) they are the three principles of the vital force in the blood: “Attraction, Circulation, Repulsion --- the Alchemical Salt, Mercury, Sulphur” [APP ¶24].

**Quoted.** Basil and Crollius: “the mercury, slat and sulfur --- spirit, body and soul --- lie hid together in one thing” [II.1 ¶11]; “there is no constant quality of any body which is not to be found in the salt, mercury, and sulfur thereof” [II.1 ¶14]. Eudoxus: they are present, seemingly but not truly united, in the apparently homogeneous Water — “Salt, Sulphur and Mercury --- which are the spirit, the soul, and the body” [IV.3 ¶7]. Note the sources differ on which principle is spirit, soul or body.

E1540.summary: In Sendivogius, a substance taken with water from Our Earth, upon which the radical moisture is put.
E1540.body: Quoted from Sendivogius: “water and salt-nitre, which comes from Our Earth” [IV.3 ¶21]; the radical moisture is put upon it. Not further explained.

E1541.summary: An unnamed author, apparently Eirenaeus (following the n37 verse), cited from Introitus Apertus cap. 7 for an explanation of the whole difficulty.
E1541.body: Cited at [IV.1 ¶43] and [IV.1 n38] (Introitus Apertus, cap. 7) for ‘an explanation of the whole difficulty’ — the Fiery Dragon, the Lodestone, purgation, and “Hence comes the Chamelion which is our Chaos”. The note itself names no author; the context suggests Eirenaeus, since ‘the same author’ follows the verse cited at n37.

E1542.summary: In Vaughan, the place of Nature's treasures, behind a Door that must be opened through knowledge of the First Matter.
E1542.body: Quoted from Vaughan: the Sanctuary of Nature is discovered by knowing the First Matter; “There is nothing between thee and her treasures but the Door: that indeed must be opened.” [III.4 ¶44].

E1543.summary: In the Appendix, the self-willed life or Will, which entraps the Light and holds the key to Sulphur's prison.
E1543.body: Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood: “Saturn or the self-willed life” [APP ¶72], “the selfish Saturnine life in man”, entraps the Light and craves more; it is overcome by satiation and then transmuted [APP ¶72]. “a Saturn (i.e., Will) has the Key to the prison where Sulphur lies bound” [APP ¶125]. As a planetary property, nothing can be felt or realized “without the voluntary dominance of Saturn and Luna” [APP ¶113]. Compare Saturnian Will and Salt of Saturn.

E1544.summary: Planetary names used in the Appendix as qualities of character and work: Saturnine dark potentiality cleared by the Jupiter element.
E1544.body: Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood, judging a work or character: “It is a Saturnine mass of power in mere potentiality; a dark cloud; chaos before Light strikes through it.” and “It wants the Jupiter element to clear it.” [APP ¶175].

forms: Saturnian Monarchy of the Freed Will
E1545.summary: Something founded on the Matter (as Pan), once circumscribed in Intellect for the manifestation of its Light; not further explained.
E1545.body: Atwood says the Matter, as Pan, is “the foundation of the great Saturnian Monarchy of the Freed Will, which was once circumscribed in Intellect, for the manifestation of its Light” [III.2 ¶7]. Not further explained.

E1546.summary: The Will, figured by the drunken Saturn of the verse, which revels without rational restraint through the subordinate faculties until sated and asleep.
E1546.body: Atwood reads the drunken Saturn of the verse as the Will: “For the Saturnian Will, being allowed to revel without limitation or rational restraint” through the subordinate faculties, until “his desires are more than satisfied, and, as the image runs, from the effect he sleeps” [III.1 ¶68]. Compare the Appendix account of Saturn as self-willed life overcome by satiation [APP ¶72].

E1547.summary: The knowledge the few wise took with them into obscurity.
E1547.body: Atwood says the wise preserved their knowledge “by burying themselves with their saving science in profound obscurity” [I.1 ¶30].

E1548.summary: Cited for the command to have Salt in ourselves and for the honour of the ass at his triumph.
E1548.body: Atwood cites the Savior's order to have Salt in ourselves, “that Salt which the Savior orders that we should have it in ourselves” [II.3 ¶54]. She also cites the Saviour's choice of the ass ‘on the occasion of his greatest earthly triumph’ to illustrate that animal's honour [III.2 ¶64].

E1549.summary: Named by Atwood with Kant and Fichte as falling short of objective realization, though ranked above them; quoted on awakening from Intellectual Intuition.
E1549.body: Atwood criticizes Kant, Fichte and Schelling for a metaphysics ending in void non-entity and skepticism, short of objective realization, while ranking Schelling above the other two [III.2 ¶31]. She cites him in support of the view that after the intuition only the remembered vision remains, owing to the limits of human reason: “We awaken from the Intellectual Intuition, says Schelling, as from a state of death” [IV.2 ¶33]. The Appendix (Table Talk, later layer) mentions him with Fichte by way of contrast [APP ¶96] and in the same list as ones who ‘saw it’ [APP ¶117].

E1550.summary: The glossator of the Scholium, Atwood's main and approved commentator in I.3, cited for practical and spiritual readings of the Hermetic text.
E1550.body: Atwood cites the Scholiast throughout I.3 with approval (‘our Scholiast’, ‘the wise Scholiast’), taking the Scholium as giving full instructions. He interprets the elements, colours, recipe, Mercury, vulture, mountain, fire and bird, “not corporally but spiritually and wisely” [I.3 n4]–[I.3 n16]. He locates the work in life — “It is prepared in the innermost chamber of life” [I.3 n48] — and glosses ‘as vinegar makes vinegar’ [I.3 n48–n55]. He supports practical readings of the Athanor and Hermetic seal — “The matter, he says, is to be decocted in the philosophic furnace called Athanor, with a continual fire.” — the treasury of nature in the breast, fixed sulfur as balsam of nature, and the soul of gold as aurific principle [I.3 n57–n67]. He is cited on entering the Spirit (“Thou must enter with thy whole spirit into the center of nature”), the repeated opening of the body, Magnesia, the essence of life as Fire, the Dragon as first blackness, secret sulfur and the rarity of the philosophic water [I.3 n19–n36]; and on the affinity of body and spirit — “The bodies of the metals, explains our Scholiast, are the domiciles of their spirits” — dissolution, multiplication and the parents nursed [I.3 n37–n42].

E1551.summary: Named only in a phrase borrowed within Vaughan's quotation.
E1551.body: Mentioned only within a quotation from Vaughan: “bad news (as the schoolmen phrase it)” [IV.2 ¶35].

E1552.summary: Listed by Atwood among the confessed adepts.
E1552.body: Named in Atwood's list of confessed adepts [I.1 ¶39].

E1553.summary: Cited by Atwood throughout as supporting authority: on Wisdom, blessing from God, purity, the conversion of darkness to light, and as analogue of the Hermetic Work.
E1553.body: Atwood cites Scripture as endorsed authority. It promises Wisdom, following Solomon's panegyric, with other such places [II.1 ¶45]; the Scriptures teach a faith bestowing Wisdom, God's sentence on the Serpent (“I will put enmity between thee and the woman”), and promises of Wisdom and material fruits, and are to be read as obscure and mystical [IV.3 ¶37–¶46]. Blessing and increase come from God: “the Lesser is blessed by the Greater”, with ‘Every good gift…’ and ‘God alone giveth the increase’; the talent is taken from him who does not use it [III.4 ¶20]. It supports the conversion of darkness into light: “The night shineth as the day, the darkness and the light are all alike to Him” [III.2 ¶10]; number, weight and measure as Nature's three dimensions: “Thou hast disposed all things, in number, weight, and measure.” [III.3 ¶67]; and that the healer must first be healed: “Prepare thy work without, and make it fit for thyself in thy field; and afterwards build thy house” [III.1 ¶9, III.1 n7] (the note refers to the Wisdom of Solomon and Proverbs 24), with the beam and mote and ‘Physician, heal thyself’. For purity she cites “He that hath clean hands and a pure heart”, saying she quotes it as apt, ‘proved on the Divine Ground’, not because it is popular [IV.1 ¶39–¶40]. The ancestors found the Word of Life, “which their neglected Scriptures everywhere testify of” [IV.2 ¶43]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer) the Work revealed in Holy Scripture is the analogue of the Hermetic Work, and the Stone of the Chief Corner Stone [APP ¶139].

E1554.summary: The Matter in its flowing, moist state, passive to every impression of the light.
E1554.body: Atwood: “In its flowing, humid state it is called the sea of the wise, passive to all impression and influences of the light” [I.3 n16].

E1555.summary: In Synesius and the New Light, the precious thing congealed in gold and silver and abiding in the sea of the world.
E1555.body: Quoted (Synesius; the New Light): the precious thing is “a ting more precious than the whole world; which I plainly tell thee is nothing else than our sea water” [I.2 ¶33]; it is congealed in gold and silver and abides ‘in the sea of the world’.

E1556.summary: In Boehme, the concealment set before the true ground of the art to prevent its misuse.
E1556.body: Quoted from Boehme: “the Seal of God lieth before it, to conceal the true ground” [II.1 ¶25], so that the art may not be misused.

E1557.summary: Greater than the first Adam: the restoration exceeds what was lost.
E1557.body: Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood: “for the second Adam is greater than the first” [APP ¶98] — the restoration exceeds what was lost.

E1558.summary: In Norton, the character of the Elixir as engendered by the concord of virtues; not further explained.
E1558.body: Quoted from Norton: from the concord of virtues “Is engendered a thing of Second Intention” [IV.2 ¶34]. Not further explained.

E1559.summary: The stage in which Nature alone works, without hands, by regulated external fire; for Atwood, the main reference of the Ordinal's period of years.
E1559.body: Eirenaeus: “In the Second, however, Nature alone operates, and without any imposition of hands” [IV.1 ¶11], by well-regulated external fire. Khunrath likewise: after the first act, in one vessel, furnace and fire, body, spirit and soul dissolve and reunite, they “rot of themselves and without manual cooperation, by the sole labors of nature” [IV.1 ¶36]. Atwood says the Ordinal's period of years: “This is meant chiefly in reference to the Second Operation” [IV.1 ¶17], linking it to the discovery of the philosophic Salt. Its relation to the Gross Work is not stated. Compare Second Work.

E1560.summary: The Paradisiacal Life, lived under the Cross.
E1560.body: Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood: “Living in the Second Principle means living the Paradisiacal Life” [APP ¶94]; it is lived under the Cross, the heart life below the extended arms representing it.

E1561.summary: In Van helmont, second qualities misleadingly trusted, contrasted with specifical (appropriated) qualities acting only on their proper object.
E1561.body: Quoted from Van helmont: those go astray who, “they too much trusting to Second qualities, as being ill secure, do sleep thereupon”, neglect the “specifical qualities, also appropriated ones (which are only extended on their proper object)” [IV.1 ¶39].

E1562.summary: In the Adept, a spirit subsisting and tinging in the body, extracted by the Preparing Spirit.
E1562.body: Quoted from the Adept: the Preparing Spirit “extracts a Second Spirit subsisting and tinging in the body”, “extracting from it the tinging spirit” [IV.1 ¶10].

E1563.summary: The continuation of the First Work, perfecting the new embryo and multiplying its light; for Atwood, the Solution of the Philosophic Salt.
E1563.body: Atwood: “the Second Work, which is only, in continuation of the First, to perfect the newly informed embryo and multiply its vivific light” [I.3 n7]. It is one of the Art's greatest subtleties: “By the Second Work we are to understand, therefore, the Solution of the Philosophic Salt” [IV.1 ¶36]. Eudoxus: “The Fourth Key of the Art is the entrance to the Second Work” [IV.3 ¶12], in which the Water is reduced to Earth. Compare Second Operation.

E1564.summary: In Eirenaeus, the fire contained in, and identified with, ‘our water’.
E1564.body: Quoted from Eirenaeus: “For in our water is our secret fire.” and “This is our water, this our secret fire.” [III.1 ¶69]; the water is apparently Mercury. Compare secret Fire of the Wise.

E1565.summary: The only agent the Art grants for purifying Nature; without knowing it, one fails even with the true matter.
E1565.body: In a passage whose voice is unclear (Atwood, or continuing ‘our author of The Triumph’, cited in the next sentence): “the secret Fire of the Wise, which is the only agent granted by Art to purify and dispose Nature to a sacrifice of her last life” [IV.2 ¶6]. Eudoxus: it makes a water that does not wet the hands run out of the dry-looking ‘plant’, and many fail “for want of knowing the secret fire of the wise” even after knowing the true matter [IV.3 ¶16]. The same paragraph names “the Understanding of Our Fire, which is both secret and natural” as one of two things that give the Keys; whether this is the same fire is not stated outright.
